idiom_name: composition over inheritance: a reference member to the delegate + forwarding member functions
implementation_notes: C++ never generates forwarding for a member object, so the classic structure is written out: the wrapper derives from the same abstract interface as the delegate, holds it by reference (or by `std::unique_ptr` when it owns it) and forwards each member explicitly. A member is the preferred replacement for private inheritance, which cppreference notes is also used to model 'implemented-in-terms-of' but is generally weaker than a member for encapsulation; forwarding itself stays justified when the wrapper must be substitutable for the delegate (Decorator, Proxy) or must add behaviour per call. Beware the separate language feature 'delegating constructors', which shares the word but forwards between constructors of one class rather than to another object.
pitfalls: Delegating constructors are a different feature - `Circle(r) : Circle{r, "black"}` forwards to another constructor, not to another object - and the two are easily conflated in review.

Storing the delegate by value slices it when it is held through the interface (only the wrapper's copy of the state is forwarded to), while storing it by reference makes the wrapper dangle if the delegate dies first.
Transparent forwarding through `operator->` hides the callee: every member access silently lands on the wrapped object, including calls the client believes it makes on the wrapper.

variants.name: Type-erased callable delegate (std::function member)
variants.implementation_notes: Where the reused behaviour is a single operation or a small closed set, the delegate does not need an interface at all: store a `std::function` (or a template parameter for the static form) and forward calls to it. This is the functional counterpart of the OO realization - the delegate is any callable, so free functions, lambdas, bound member functions and function objects all qualify - and it avoids a vtable and a wrapper class hierarchy at the cost of type erasure, a possible heap allocation for large captures and an exception on empty invocation (`std::bad_function_call`). Prefer it when the delegated thing is a verb, not an object.
pitfalls: An empty `std::function` throws `std::bad_function_call`; a default-constructed or moved-from delegate must be guarded or checked before the call.
Type erasure hides the callee from the compiler: inlining and devirtualisation are lost for all but trivial targets, and capture-heavy lambdas allocate.
One `std::function` cannot express a multi-method interface; use the interface realization when the delegate must expose several related operations.
